stories.title: Australians missing in Nepal targeted by ‘heartbreaking’ and ‘abhorrent’ racist slurs
stories.summary: As families await news after the catastrophe, community members appeal for compassion in the face of hateful rhetoric A slew of racist social media comments have been made towards Australians missing in the catastrophic Nepal-Tibet floods , prompting calls for greater accountability of major platforms to remove hateful rhetoric. On Monday, the total number of Australians missing after flash floods triggered by a massive glacier collapse in the Himalayas rose to 43, and the overall death toll was at least 810 people. stories.title: FIFA president Infantino ‘must go’, says former UEFA boss Platini
stories.summary: In a scathing interview, French great Michel Platini accuses Infantino of always loving ‘money and power’. French football great Michel Platini says FIFA president Gianni Infantino “must go” following the scandals that have surrounded football’s governing body and rocked the sport globally. “Economic affairs are one thing, but Infantino has failed because he is the guarantor of the rules of the game and he didn’t respect them,” former UEFA president Platini told a French media outlet on Sunday. The 56-year-old Infantino has been under fire since his aborted plan to bring private investment into FIFA events, such as the World Cup. He was also lambasted over a number of controversies during the recently concluded World Cup in North America. He also pointed to the half-time show during the final, which largely overran the required maximum of 15 minutes, and the furore around FIFA suspending the red card ban given to American forward Folarin Balogun following a phone call made by United States President Donald Trump to Infantino. “The ad breaks are not in the rules, the 30-minute half-time break in the final is not in the rules, and the red card, that’s the worst,” said Platini. “He’s the guarantor [of the rules], he doesn’t respect them, he must go,” added Platini, who was UEFA’s secretary-general under the Frenchman’s leadership. Since the World Cup, UEFA threatened to boycott FIFA tournaments until Infantino scrapped the FIFA Forward Enterprises plan to bring in private investment. European football’s governing body UEFA has also accused Infantino of “criminal mismanagement” over the private financing. FIFA did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for a comment. Other regional bodies – the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF) and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) – have joined UEFA in putting pressure on Infantino, who is hoping to run for re-election in March.

stories.title: 'They wrote little letters': How kids in Portugal are making money off their neighbours' plastic waste
stories.summary: The first ever bottle deposit return scheme in southern Europe is helping the environment - and funding kids' bucket list trips. Sisters Ariela and Alice had already been using Portugal's bottle return scheme to earn money but since June they have upped the ante: now instead of just returning their own bottles, they are asking their neighbours' for their plastic waste and making money off that too. Since April this year, when the Volta scheme launched, plastic bottles in Portugal have a €0.10 deposit added to the cost. If you return the empty bottle to a supermarket with a Volta machine, you're given a receipt which can be exchanged for discounts or cash. "They wrote little letters and I printed them with their project and the time when they were going to collect the bag," explains their mother, Karina Lauro, who moved to Portugal from Rio de Janeiro in 2024. "They leave the bag at people's doors and every day, at nine o'clock in the evening, they go back to pick up that bag with the bottles, when there are any." The empty bottles are then exchanged for money. With a clear goal: by June next year they aim to collect 120,000 bottles so they can make €6,000 each. It was the girls who came up with the idea of using Volta to raise funds and to involve the neighbours, after their mother warned them that just using the bottles from home would not make them much money. "It was very little, wasn't it? Because it was just the bottles from our house," says Karina Lauro. "Basically, if it were only us, there would be no way."

stories.title: Hybe chairman to be referred to prosecution over alleged deception of shareholders: police
stories.summary: SEOUL, Aug. 31 (Yonhap) -- Bang Si-hyuk, chairman of K-pop powerhouse Hybe, will...
article_sentences: Bang Si-hyuk, chairman of K-pop powerhouse Hybe, will be referred to the prosecution this week for possible indictment on suspicion of deceiving investors into selling their stakes in his company, police said Monday.
"We plan to forward the case to the prosecution within the week," Hong Seok-ki, head of the National Office of Investigation, told a press briefing.

Bang is accused of violating the Capital Markets Act by deceiving investors into selling their stakes in Hybe in 2019, just before the company went public, making nearly 200 billion won (US$145 million) in additional and illegal profits.
Police launched an investigation into the allegations in December 2024 and began a full-scale probe in July of last year, which included a raid on Hybe headquarters.
Their investigation was prolonged after the prosecution requested supplementary investigations while rejecting two arrest warrant requests filed by the police.
Sources close to the issue said the police were expected to refer Bang's case to the prosecution without seeking his detention.
